title: Bilinear and Quadratic Forms
---

Inner products are symmetric bilinear forms with an extra positivity condition. We now drop positivity and classify symmetric bilinear forms themselves. Throughout this section, $V$ is a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $k$ with $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$ (characteristic $2$ appears only in a note), and $B$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $V$.

## <span class="num">9.6.1</span> Quadratic Forms and Polarization

:::definition{9.6.1} Quadratic form
A ***quadratic form*** on $V$ is a function $Q : V \to k$ of the form $Q(v) = B(v, v)$ for some bilinear form $B$ on $V$. If $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$ is a basis and $A = (a_{ij})$ is the matrix of $B$, then $$Q\Big(\sum_i x_i e_i\Big) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij} x_i x_j = x^t A x,$$ a homogeneous polynomial of degree $2$ in the coordinates.
:::

:::proposition{9.6.2} Polarization
Let $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$. If $B$ is a symmetric bilinear form and $Q(v) = B(v, v)$, then $$B(u, v) = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(Q(u + v) - Q(u) - Q(v)\big) \quad \text{for all } u, v \in V.$$ Consequently, $B \mapsto Q$ is a bijection from symmetric bilinear forms on $V$ to quadratic forms on $V$.
:::

:::proof
Expanding, $Q(u + v) = B(u, u) + B(u, v) + B(v, u) + B(v, v) = Q(u) + Q(v) + 2B(u, v)$, and we may divide by $2$. So $Q$ determines $B$, and the map is injective. For surjectivity, let $Q(v) = B'(v, v)$ for some bilinear form $B'$. Then $B(u, v) = \frac{1}{2}(B'(u, v) + B'(v, u))$ is a symmetric bilinear form with $B(v, v) = B'(v, v) = Q(v)$.
:::

:::example{9.6.3} A quadratic form and its matrix
On $k^2$, the quadratic form $Q(x, y) = x^2 + 4xy - y^2$ corresponds to the symmetric matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{psmallmatrix}$, i.e., to the symmetric bilinear form $$B((x, y), (x', y')) = xx' + 2xy' + 2yx' - yy'.$$ The cross term $4xy$ is split equally between the two off-diagonal entries.
:::

:::note
In characteristic $2$, polarization fails, and so does the classification below. Over $\FF_2$, the form $B(x, y) = x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1$ on $\FF_2^2$ is symmetric and nonzero, but $B(v, v) = 2x_1 x_2 = 0$ for every $v$, so it has the same quadratic form as the zero form. It also has no orthogonal basis in the sense of Theorem [9.6](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms) below: in such a basis its matrix would be diagonal with entries $B(e_i, e_i) = 0$, i.e., zero.
:::

## <span class="num">9.6.2</span> Orthogonal Bases

To classify symmetric bilinear forms, we look for a vector $v$ with $B(v, v) \neq 0$ and then pass to $\operatorname{span}(v)^\perp$, as in the inductive construction of orthonormal bases.

:::lemma{9.6.4} Anisotropic vectors exist
If $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$ and $B \neq 0$ is symmetric, then there is $v \in V$ with $B(v, v) \neq 0$.
:::

:::proof
Choose $u, w$ with $B(u, w) \neq 0$. By polarization, $2B(u, w) = Q(u + w) - Q(u) - Q(w) \neq 0$, so at least one of $Q(u + w)$, $Q(u)$, $Q(w)$ is nonzero.
:::

:::lemma{9.6.5} Splitting off a vector
If $B(v, v) \neq 0$, then $V = \operatorname{span}(v) \oplus v^\perp$, where $v^\perp = \{w \in V : B(w, v) = 0\}$.
:::

:::proof
The linear functional $B(v, \cdot)$ is nonzero (its value at $v$ is $B(v, v) \neq 0$), and since $B$ is symmetric its kernel is $v^\perp$, which therefore has dimension $\dim V - 1$. If $cv \in v^\perp$, then $cB(v, v) = 0$, so $c = 0$; hence $\operatorname{span}(v) \cap v^\perp = \{0\}$, and the dimensions add up to $\dim V$. Explicitly, $w = \frac{B(v, w)}{B(v, v)} v + \big(w - \frac{B(v, w)}{B(v, v)} v\big)$.
:::

:::theorem{9.6.6} Orthogonal bases for symmetric forms
Let $\operatorname{char} k \neq 2$ and let $B$ be a symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional space $V$. Then $V$ has an ***orthogonal basis*** for $B$: a basis $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$ with $B(e_i, e_j) = 0$ for $i \neq j$. Equivalently, for every symmetric matrix $A \in \mcM_{n \times n}(k)$ there is an invertible $P$ such that $P^t A P$ is diagonal.
:::

:::proof
Induction on $n = \dim V$. If $n = 0$ or $B = 0$, any basis works. Otherwise, Lemma [9.6.4](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#lemma-9-6-4) gives $e_1$ with $B(e_1, e_1) \neq 0$, and Lemma [9.6.5](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#lemma-9-6-5) gives $V = \operatorname{span}(e_1) \oplus W$ with $W = e_1^\perp$ of dimension $n - 1$. The restriction of $B$ to $W$ is symmetric and bilinear, so by induction $W$ has a basis $\{e_2, \ldots, e_n\}$ with $B(e_i, e_j) = 0$ for $2 \leq i \neq j$. Also $B(e_j, e_1) = B(e_1, e_j) = 0$ for $j \geq 2$, since $e_j \in W$. So $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$ is an orthogonal basis.

For the matrix statement, apply this to the form $B(x, y) = x^t A y$ on $k^n$ and let $P$ be the matrix whose columns are the $e_i$; by Proposition [9.1.6](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-6), $P^t A P$ is the (diagonal) matrix of $B$ in the basis $\{e_i\}$.
:::

:::note
In an orthogonal basis the matrix of $B$ is $\diag(d_1, \ldots, d_n)$ with $d_i = B(e_i, e_i)$. So the rank of $B$ is the number of nonzero $d_i$, and $B$ is nondegenerate iff every $d_i \neq 0$. The $d_i$ themselves are not determined by $B$: replacing $e_i$ by $c e_i$ ($c \neq 0$) replaces $d_i$ by $c^2 d_i$. The classification problem is to decide how far the $d_i$ can be normalized, and this depends on which elements of $k$ are squares.
:::

## <span class="num">9.6.3</span> Classification over $\CC$ and over $\RR$

To state the classification, we say that a bilinear form $B$ on $V$ and a bilinear form $B'$ on $V'$ are ***equivalent*** if there is a linear isomorphism $T : V \to V'$ with $B'(T(u), T(v)) = B(u, v)$ for all $u, v \in V$. By Proposition [9.1.6](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#proposition-9-1-6), two forms on the same space are equivalent iff their matrices in a fixed basis are congruent; and every form on an $n$-dimensional space is equivalent, via a coordinate isomorphism, to the form $x^t A y$ on $k^n$, where $A$ is its matrix in some basis.

Over $\CC$, every number is a square, so everything can be normalized.

:::theorem{9.6.7} Symmetric forms over $\CC$
Let $B$ be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$. Then $V$ has a basis $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$ with $$B(e_i, e_j) = \delta_{ij},$$ i.e., the matrix of $B$ is the identity. In particular, any two nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms on complex vector spaces of the same finite dimension are equivalent.
:::

:::proof
Let $\{f_1, \ldots, f_n\}$ be an orthogonal basis (Theorem [9.6.6](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#theorem-9-6-6)) and $d_i = B(f_i, f_i)$, which is nonzero because $B$ is nondegenerate. Choose $c_i \in \CC$ with $c_i^2 = d_i$, and set $e_i = f_i / c_i$. Then $B(e_i, e_i) = d_i / c_i^2 = 1$, and $B(e_i, e_j) = 0$ for $i \neq j$.
:::

:::note
Over $\CC$, symmetric bilinear forms have little to do with geometry: the form $B(z, w) = \sum z_i w_i$ on $\CC^n$ (whose matrix is $I$) has $B(v, v) = 0$ for $v = (1, i, 0, \ldots, 0)$. The forms that measure lengths over $\CC$ are the Hermitian ones. The same proof shows that a possibly degenerate symmetric form on a complex space has, in a suitable basis, the matrix $\diag(I_r, 0)$, where $r$ is its rank.
:::

Over $\RR$, only nonnegative numbers are squares, so the best we can do is normalize each $d_i$ to $\pm 1$.

:::theorem{9.6.8} Symmetric forms over $\RR$
Let $B$ be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form on a real vector space $V$ of dimension $n$. Then there is an integer $p$ with $0 \leq p \leq n$ and a basis $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$ with $B(e_i, e_j) = 0$ for $i \neq j$, $B(e_i, e_i) = 1$ for $i \leq p$, and $B(e_i, e_i) = -1$ for $i > p$. That is, $$B\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i e_i, \sum_{i=1}^n y_i e_i\Big) = \sum_{i=1}^{p} x_i y_i - \sum_{i=p+1}^{n} x_i y_i, \qquad \text{matrix } \begin{pmatrix} I_p & 0 \\ 0 & -I_{n-p} \end{pmatrix}.$$
:::

:::proof
Let $\{f_1, \ldots, f_n\}$ be an orthogonal basis with $d_i = B(f_i, f_i) \neq 0$, and set $e_i = f_i / \sqrt{|d_i|}$. Then $B(e_i, e_i) = d_i / |d_i| = \pm 1$. Reorder the basis so that the $+1$’s come first.
:::

The number $p$ does not depend on the basis. This is *Sylvester’s law of inertia*.

:::theorem{9.6.9} Sylvester’s law of inertia
In Theorem [9.6.8](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#theorem-9-6-8), $p$ is the largest dimension of a subspace $W \subseteq V$ on which $B$ is positive-definite ($B(w, w) > 0$ for all nonzero $w \in W$), and $n - p$ is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $B$ is negative-definite. In particular, $p$ is the same for every basis as in Theorem [9.6.8](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#theorem-9-6-8).
:::

:::proof
Let $$V_+ = \operatorname{span}(e_1, \ldots, e_p), \qquad V_- = \operatorname{span}(e_{p+1}, \ldots, e_n).$$ For $v = \sum_{i \leq p} x_i e_i \in V_+$, $B(v, v) = \sum_{i \leq p} x_i^2 > 0$ unless $v = 0$, so $B$ is positive-definite on $V_+$, a subspace of dimension $p$.

Now let $W$ be any subspace on which $B$ is positive-definite. For $v = \sum_{i > p} x_i e_i \in V_-$, $B(v, v) = -\sum_{i > p} x_i^2 \leq 0$. A nonzero vector of $W \cap V_-$ would satisfy both $B(v, v) > 0$ and $B(v, v) \leq 0$; so $W \cap V_- = \{0\}$. Hence $$\dim W + (n - p) = \dim W + \dim V_- = \dim(W + V_-) \leq n,$$ and $\dim W \leq p$. So $p$ is the largest dimension of a positive-definite subspace, which is defined without reference to any basis. Applying this to the form $-B$, whose basis as in Theorem [9.6.8](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#theorem-9-6-8) is $e_{p+1}, \ldots, e_n, e_1, \ldots, e_p$, shows that $n - p$ is the largest dimension of a negative-definite subspace.
:::

:::definition{9.6.10} Signature
The ***signature*** of a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form $B$ on a real vector space of dimension $n$ is the pair $(p, q)$ with $q = n - p$, where $p$ and $q$ are as in Sylvester’s law of inertia.
:::

:::corollary{9.6.11} Classification over $\RR$
Let $B$ and $B'$ be nondegenerate symmetric bilinear forms on real vector spaces $V$ and $V'$ of the same finite dimension. Then $B$ and $B'$ are equivalent if and only if they have the same signature.
:::

:::proof
If both have signature $(p, q)$, take bases $\{e_i\}$ of $V$ for $B$ and $\{e_i'\}$ of $V'$ for $B'$ as in Theorem [9.6.8](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#theorem-9-6-8), and let $T : V \to V'$ be the linear isomorphism with $T(e_i) = e_i'$; then $B'(T(e_i), T(e_j)) = B(e_i, e_j)$ for all $i, j$, hence $B'(T(u), T(v)) = B(u, v)$ for all $u, v$ by bilinearity. Conversely, if $T$ is an isomorphism with $B'(T(u), T(v)) = B(u, v)$, it maps subspaces on which $B$ is positive-definite to subspaces of the same dimension on which $B'$ is positive-definite, and $T^{-1}$ does the reverse; so the largest such dimensions agree.
:::

:::example{9.6.12} Signatures
- An inner product on $\RR^n$ has signature $(n, 0)$; conversely, a form of signature $(n, 0)$ is positive-definite. So Theorem [9.6.8](/notes/math-55a/9-6-bilinear-and-quadratic-forms#theorem-9-6-8) with $p = n$ recovers the existence of orthonormal bases.
- The Minkowski form $v_1 w_1 - v_2 w_2 - v_3 w_3 - v_4 w_4$ on $\RR^4$ has signature $(1, 3)$.
- The quadratic form $Q(x, y) = xy$ on $\RR^2$ comes from $B((x, y), (x', y')) = \frac{1}{2}(xy' + yx')$. In the basis $e_1 = (1, 1)$, $e_2 = (1, -1)$, we have $B(e_1, e_1) = 1$, $B(e_2, e_2) = -1$, and $B(e_1, e_2) = \frac{1}{2}(-1 + 1) = 0$. So the signature is $(1, 1)$; in coordinates, $xy = \big(\frac{x + y}{2}\big)^2 - \big(\frac{x - y}{2}\big)^2$.
:::

:::note
Two practical remarks. First, by the real spectral theorem, a real symmetric matrix $A$ can be diagonalized by a matrix $P$ with $P^t = P^{-1}$, so $P^t A P = \diag(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)$ is simultaneously the matrix of the operator $x \mapsto Ax$ and of the form $x^t A y$ in the new basis. Hence the signature of $x^t A y$ is (number of positive eigenvalues of $A$, number of negative eigenvalues of $A$). Second, since $\det(P^t A P) = \det(P)^2 \det(A)$, the sign of $\det A$ is $(-1)^q$. For degenerate forms the same argument as in Sylvester’s law shows that the numbers $p$ and $q$ of $+1$’s and $-1$’s in a diagonal form are well defined, with $p + q = \rank B$.
:::

## <span class="num">9.6.4</span> Forms over the Rationals

Over $\QQ$, much less can be normalized, because few rational numbers are squares, and number theory enters. The following example shows that the values a form takes can distinguish two forms that look alike.

:::example{9.6.13} Two forms over $\QQ$
Let $B$ and $B'$ be the forms on $\QQ^2$ with matrices $$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix},$$ so $Q(v) = v_1^2 + v_2^2$ and $Q'(v) = 2v_1^2 + v_2^2$. Both are nondegenerate, and over $\RR$ both have signature $(2, 0)$.

**$Q'$ takes the value $3$:** $Q'(1, 1) = 3$.

**$Q$ does not take the value $3$:** suppose $v_1^2 + v_2^2 = 3$ with $v \in \QQ^2$. Clearing denominators, $n_1^2 + n_2^2 = 3m^2$ with integers $n_1, n_2, m$, $m \neq 0$, and we may assume they have no common factor. Squares of integers are $0$ or $1 \bmod 4$, so $n_1^2 + n_2^2 \equiv 0, 1, 2 \pmod 4$, while $3m^2 \equiv 0, 3 \pmod 4$. Hence both sides are $\equiv 0 \pmod 4$. Then $m$ is even (an odd $m$ would give $3m^2 \equiv 3$), and $n_1^2 + n_2^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ forces $n_1$ and $n_2$ to be even. This contradicts the assumption that they have no common factor.

**So $B$ and $B'$ are not equivalent over $\QQ$:** if $T : \QQ^2 \to \QQ^2$ were a linear isomorphism with $B(T(u), T(v)) = B'(u, v)$, then $Q(T(1, 1)) = Q'(1, 1) = 3$, which is impossible.
:::
